title: "Populations and samples"

Suppose we calculate the proportion of personal-pronoun tokens in UD Turkish BOUN whose annotation has `Case=Acc`. Which population does that number describe? One answer is immediate: it describes the qualifying annotated tokens in this release. A claim about personal-pronoun use in written Turkish would go further, since most Turkish documents and sentences had no route into the treebank. It would also assume that the UD annotation tracks the use of accusative case that the linguistic claim concerns.

The basic idea is that a population is defined by both its units and the process that could make those units observable. Two selection steps matter here. Written sentences first entered the treebank, and our filter then selected particular annotated tokens from those sentences. We will keep the steps separate so that we can tell when a number describes the finite resource and when it is being used to estimate a quantity in a broader process of Turkish usage.

## A finite linguistic population

We begin with [UD Turkish BOUN, release 2.18](https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/tr_boun/), a Universal Dependencies treebank for Turkish, a Turkic language. Türk et al. ([2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-021-09558-0)) describe the source and annotation process, while Marşan et al. ([2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11782)) document the agglutination-sensitive revisions. The release contains written sentences sampled within five selected Turkish National Corpus registers. Native-speaker linguists manually annotated and cross-checked automatically preprocessed material.

We restrict the treebank to tokens tagged `UPOS=PRON` and `PronType=Prs` with an attested UD `Case` value. This restriction gives the personal-pronoun case population used below; it excludes other pronouns and tokens without a recorded case value. One row is one annotated token nested in a sampled sentence. The release is CC BY-SA 4.0, subject to the upstream permission conditions described in the [Turkish National Corpus paper](https://aclanthology.org/L12-1590/).

```{r}
#| label: load-ud-population
library(ggplot2)

pronouns <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/personal-pronoun-cases.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

case_counts <- as.data.frame(table(case = pronouns$case))
names(case_counts)[2] <- "tokens"
case_counts$proportion <- case_counts$tokens / sum(case_counts$tokens)
case_counts <- case_counts[order(case_counts$tokens), ]

stopifnot(
  nrow(pronouns) == 2128L,
  length(unique(pronouns$sentence_id)) == 1727L,
  sum(pronouns$accusative) == 430L
)

case_counts
```

This table contains every row in BOUN 2.18 that satisfies the course filter. The
filter selects tokens annotated `UPOS=PRON`, `PronType=Prs`, and one of the eight
attested UD `Case` values. Its `r format(nrow(pronouns), big.mark = ",")` rows therefore describe that annotated subset;
they do not include personal-pronoun expressions outside the filter or tokens that
were never part of the source sentences.

The first source-ordered row makes the unit concrete: it records one token form, its sentence identifier and sentence text, its UD case label, its register, and the derived `accusative` indicator. The sentence is the source selection context; the token is the row being analyzed. This is the unit-versus-container distinction introduced in [linguistic data](../foundations/linguistic-data.qmd#unit-and-observation-key).

```{r}
#| label: show-ud-source-row
pronouns[1L, c(
  "register", "sentence_id", "sentence_text", "form", "case", "accusative"
)]
```

## Defining the objects

A [**target population**](https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-1-definitions-of-statistics-probability-and-key-terms) is the collection of units about which an inference is intended. A [**sample**](https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-1-definitions-of-statistics-probability-and-key-terms) is the collection observed through a particular selection process. A fixed numerical feature of a modeled population is a [**parameter**](https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-1-definitions-of-statistics-probability-and-key-terms); the rule used to calculate a candidate value from a random sample is an **estimator**; and its realized value is an [**estimate**](https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-1-definitions-of-statistics-probability-and-key-terms). The later [estimator-properties page](properties-of-estimators.qmd#estimators-are-random-variables) develops why the rule is random before the sample is observed.

For a binary indicator $X_i$ that equals one when token $i$ bears `Case=Acc`, the finite-release proportion is

$$
p_{\mathcal R}
=\frac{1}{N_{\mathcal R}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathcal R}}X_i,
$$

where $\mathcal R$ denotes this release and $N_{\mathcal R}$ is its number of qualifying token rows. The code computes that finite-population parameter directly.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-ud-population
release_size <- nrow(pronouns)
accusative_tokens <- sum(pronouns$accusative)
release_accusative_proportion <- mean(pronouns$accusative)

data.frame(
  qualifying_tokens = release_size,
  sentences_represented = length(unique(pronouns$sentence_id)),
  registers = length(unique(pronouns$register)),
  accusative_tokens = accusative_tokens,
  accusative_proportion = release_accusative_proportion
)
```

Thus $p_{\mathcal R}=$ `r sprintf("%.4f", release_accusative_proportion)` for the
qualifying rows in BOUN 2.18. There is no sampling uncertainty about this
arithmetic once the version and filtering rule are fixed.

```{r}
#| label: plot-ud-cases
#| fig-cap: "Case counts among personal-pronoun tokens in UD Turkish BOUN 2.18."
ggplot(case_counts, aes(tokens, reorder(case, tokens))) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey45", width = 0.72) +
  labs(x = "Personal-pronoun tokens", y = "UD Case value") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## The route from sampled sentences to the claim {#boun-sample-to-claim-map}

The source design selected approximately two thousand sentences within each of
five written registers: essays, broadsheet newspapers, instructional texts,
popular-culture articles, and biographies. The course preparation then searched
those sentences for tokens satisfying the pronoun-and-case filter above. This
produces the following sample-to-claim map.

| Stage | What happened | Consequence for the analysis |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Source collection | Sentences were sampled within five selected written registers. | The release represents those registers; it contains no spoken conversation and supplies no prevalence weights for Turkish usage. |
| Annotation and filtering | Linguists annotated UD features; the course filter retained case-annotated personal-pronoun tokens. | The response concerns source UD labels among qualifying tokens, not every personal-pronoun expression. |
| Analysis row | One row is one retained token; `r format(nrow(pronouns), big.mark = ",")` rows occur in `r format(length(unique(pronouns$sentence_id)), big.mark = ",")` sentences. | Two tokens from the same sentence share topic, syntax, and local context, so they do not contribute wholly separate information. |
| Narrow target | The denominator is all qualifying rows in BOUN 2.18. | The displayed proportion exactly describes this prepared table. |
| Broader target | A usage target would concern tokens from a specified Turkish production process. | Generalization would require a sampling model for registers, documents, sentences, speakers, and annotation. |

Two different claims consequently require different targets:

1. The finite-release claim concerns the qualifying annotated tokens in BOUN 2.18. The code above identifies its parameter exactly.
2. A usage claim concerns tokens that could arise from a specified Turkish production process. Connecting the release to that process requires a sampling model and assumptions about registers, sentences, and annotation.

More token rows sharpen the description of this table. They do not add spoken
settings, unrepresented registers, or known selection probabilities, so they do
not by themselves strengthen the connection to Turkish usage.

::: {.callout-warning title="Name the denominator"}
For the finite-table question, the denominator is the 2,128 qualifying rows in
BOUN 2.18. For a Turkish-usage question, the denominator would have to come from a
defined production and sampling process. The current design supplies the first
denominator and leaves the second unspecified.
:::

## Recap and forward link

1. A population is defined by both its units and the claim made about them.
2. The BOUN 2.18 proportion is known once the version and filter are fixed.
3. The same arithmetic becomes an estimate only after a broader target and sampling model are posited.

The [independent-sampling page](independent-sampling.qmd#identical-distributions-and-independence) states one such working model while retaining the row hierarchy.

## Check your understanding

1. What is the observational unit in `pronouns`, and what was the source selection unit?
2. Why is the computed proportion a parameter of the analyzed BOUN table but only an estimate for a broader usage process?
3. Which identifiers reveal dependence among token rows?
4. What additional design information would be needed to generalize to spoken Turkish?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. One row is an annotated personal-pronoun token; the source design selected sentences within five written registers. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The release and filter fix all qualifying rows, so the proportion is a known release parameter. A broader usage claim requires a sampling model, making the same quantity an estimate. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Repeated `sentence_id` values show that token rows are nested within sentences; `register` also marks a shared source context. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. We would need a spoken-language sampling frame, selection probabilities for speakers and speech settings, and identifiers for speaker, conversation, and recording dependence. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
